title: #Coronavirus on TikTok: User engagement with misinformation as a potential threat to public health behavior
screen_reason: Retrospective content analysis of 166 English-language TikTok videos retrieved under #coronavirus, each graded for misinformation against an expert-built codebook reflecting COVID-19 public health guidance. The share of the video sample containing misinformation is reported with its denominator (47/166 = 28%, split into 36 moderate and 11 high). The denominator is all items in the retrieved sample, so this is CONTENT.

estimates.country: Not stated; English-language TikTok videos (authors US-based, University of Maryland)
estimates.date: Videos published 14 March 2020 to 22 August 2020; hashtag search and download in September 2020
estimates.measure_type: % of #coronavirus TikTok videos graded as containing at least moderate-level COVID-19 misinformation
estimates.value_raw: 47/166 (28%), comprising 36 moderate + 11 high; misinformation absent in 119 (72%)
estimates.denominator: 166 English-language, publicly viewable, COVID-relevant TikTok videos under #coronavirus (166 of 1,000 videos identified in the initial search met inclusion criteria)
estimates.definition: A video counted in the numerator if reviewers graded misinformation as present at moderate or high level, judged against a codebook reflecting COVID-19 public health guidance; videos graded 'absent' (or low, which is not reported separately) are the complement. Examples: 'recommendations for quarantine were the result of a conspiracy'; 'masks do not offer protection against infection'.
estimates.misinfo_def: "Misinformation includes misleading or false information that contradicts scientific consensus."
estimates.page_loc: p. 3, Results, first paragraph; same counts in Table 1 (Misinformation: Absent 119 (72), Moderate 36 (22), High 11 (7)) and in the Discussion ('28% of videos contained at least moderate-level misinformation')
estimates.ground_truth_detail: Codebook developed by a hospital epidemiologist with infectious-disease expertise (JB) and a clinician with social-media research expertise (RM), reflecting public health guidance on COVID-19. Four reviewers (RB, JF, DS, RM) annotated videos between September 2020 and January 2021; the first 9 videos were coded by all reviewers and discrepancies adjudicated until interrater consistency exceeded 90%, after which videos were reviewed independently. No kappa reported.
estimates.moderator_quote: We retrospectively reviewed a random sample of user-created videos
estimates.notes: Single-topic hashtag corpus (#coronavirus), so denom_scope=topical. denom_selection left empty because the authors describe the 1,000-video pool as a 'random sample' of hashtag-associated videos rather than a top-N or most-viewed cut; they nonetheless concede the TikTok algorithm may have selectively displayed or suppressed videos, so an adjudicator could defensibly set denom_selection=curated. Two internal inconsistencies to flag: the abstract dates the download 20 September 2020 while Methods gives the search date as 1 September 2020; and Table 1 lists 8 healthcare-worker + 13 foundation/government + 4 news-media videos with percentages 5/4/2 that do not reconcile with 'Any official source 26 (16)'. Neither affects the 47/166 figure. The grading scale had a 'low' level that is never reported separately, so 28% is an at-least-moderate threshold, not all misinformation of any degree.

estimates.country: Not stated; English-language TikTok videos (authors US-based, University of Maryland)
estimates.date: Videos published 14 March 2020 to 22 August 2020; hashtag search and download in September 2020
estimates.measure_type: % of #coronavirus TikTok videos graded as containing HIGH-level COVID-19 misinformation (stricter threshold)
estimates.denominator: 166 English-language, publicly viewable, COVID-relevant TikTok videos under #coronavirus
estimates.definition: A video counted only if misinformation was graded HIGH based on the extent and degree of misinformation, e.g. a video implying surgical masks were contaminated with COVID-19 because they originated in China, 'only older people are at risk', 'minors cannot be infected', 'ability to hold breath means no infection'.
estimates.misinfo_def: "Misinformation includes misleading or false information that contradicts scientific consensus."
estimates.page_loc: p. 3, Table 1 (Video views by characteristic and content), Misinformation block; also stated in the Abstract
estimates.ground_truth_detail: Same expert codebook and four-reviewer procedure as the at-least-moderate row; interrater consistency above 90% on the 9-video training set before independent review.
estimates.moderator_quote: We retrospectively reviewed a random sample of user-created videos
estimates.notes: Stricter veracity threshold on the same 166-video denominator as the 28% row, hence definition_variant=true; the two rows must not be pooled together. The high band is the paper's own severity ceiling and its exemplars are flatly false claims, so breadth=false here versus misleading for the pooled at-least-moderate row. The 22% moderate-only band is deliberately not given its own row: it is a middle stratum, not a nested threshold, and 28% and 7% already bracket the definitional range.

missed_or_uncertain: Not extracted: (1) the DISCERN and PEMAT quality ratings in Table 1 (DISCERN low 50 (30%), moderate 84 (51%), high 32 (19%); PEMAT high understandability 110 (66%), high actionability 15 (9%)) — these are quality-scale bands with no truth judgement, so under §3 they are construct QUALITY; I left them out because the paper already yields direct CONTENT estimates and a QUALITY row would add nothing but noise, but an adjudicator who wants QUALITY rows recorded wherever they appear can add 'DISCERN low = 50/166 (30%)'. (2) The 22% moderate-only band (36/166), a middle stratum rather than a nested threshold. (3) '25 videos containing misinformation (15.1%)' — that is the share of all 166 videos that both contained misinformation and drew behaviour-change comments, a joint outcome, not a misinformation prevalence. (4) 'One in 4 misinformative videos elicited comments indicating intention to change behavior' and the Figure 1 within-misinformation comment shares (13 (36%) of moderate videos, 9 of 11 (82%) of high videos, etc.) — denominators are the misinformation subsets and the numerators are comment behaviours, not falsity. (5) Median view counts (8.4M overall, 6.8M moderate, 9.4M high, 7.4M any misinformation) — counts, not shares, and views here are a property of videos rather than a measured audience diet, so they do not support an EXPOSURE row. (6) All regression output (IRRs, ORs). (7) The cumulative hashtag view counts (#coronavirus 97.8 billion etc.) are platform-reported totals used to choose the hashtag, not estimates.

rob.design: Retrospective content analysis of a sample of user-created TikTok videos under #coronavirus, downloaded with an open-source TikTok scraper via TikTok's Web API on a single day in September 2020 to give a snapshot; English-language only, published on or before the search date; videos excluded if private/unviewable or unrelated to COVID-19; 1,000 videos identified, 166 (17%) eligible, published 14 March to 22 August 2020. No response rate applies. Codebook written by an infectious-disease hospital epidemiologist and a social-media clinician from public health guidance; four reviewers annotated between September 2020 and January 2021, first 9 videos coded by all with discrepancies adjudicated until interrater consistency exceeded 90%, then independent review; no kappa reported and no formal reliability subsample. Authors' own limitations: possible algorithmic selection by TikTok, English-only, human rather than automated coding.
